title: Durable, safe resetting of dysfunctional energy-balance regulation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a time-limited endocrine intervention that leaves a person’s energy-balance regulation in a durably healthier state after treatment ends. Success would mean persistent improvements in weight-related metabolic health while maintaining adequate nutrition, tolerable hunger and appropriate responses to changes in food availability. The intended advance is a lasting change in regulation, rather than weight loss that depends on continuing treatment.

The supplied research uses a working framework in which brain, gut, adipose tissue and hormonal signals interact to regulate energy balance, with potentially different mechanisms contributing in different people. The retained evidence does not independently substantiate that framework or identify a mechanism that can be durably altered. Here, “resetting” names the proposed functional outcome; it does not presume that everyone has a single biological weight setting that can be adjusted.

significance.text: As a conditional consequence of the proposed capability, a brief intervention with lasting benefits could change long-term management of obesity and related metabolic dysfunction. It could reduce the need for continuing medication to maintain those benefits and shift treatment toward establishing a healthier, self-maintaining regulatory state. Whether it would actually reduce treatment burden would depend on durability, adverse effects, retreatment requirements and the complexity of delivering the intervention.

The revolutionary feature would be persistence combined with adaptive regulation. A lower weight alone would not establish success if maintaining it involved nutritional inadequacy, excessive hunger, psychological harm or an impaired response to food scarcity. The useful analogy is restoration of healthier regulation, but that analogy must not imply a single universal set point, an identical target for every person or permanent immunity to future metabolic disease.

Downstream benefits such as fewer cardiovascular events or other disease complications are possibilities, not demonstrated consequences of this hypothetical intervention. They would require their own outcome studies. Even convincing weight and metabolic results would not establish every anticipated health benefit, applicability to every cause of obesity or safety in every population.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability, as defined by this proposal, is to identify and alter mechanisms that sustain a harmful energy-balance state so that the improvement persists after a time-limited intervention. The supplied material does not establish which mechanisms would be suitable targets, whether they differ between patient groups or whether changing them would trigger compensatory hunger or other responses that undermine the benefit. Its empty freshness record also prevents a comprehensive claim about how far the field has progressed toward this capability.

A concrete scientific barrier is demonstrating that an intervention changes regulation itself. Persistent weight loss could reflect sustained changes in behavior, anatomy, treatment exposure or other influences. A convincing mechanistic account would need to distinguish these explanations and connect the intervention to a lasting change in how appetite, energy expenditure or other relevant responses adapt to changing conditions. These are proposed research requirements; the supplied evidence identifies no validated mechanism for accomplishing them.

The engineering challenge is to produce a durable effect without making regulation dangerously inflexible. A candidate intervention would need a controllable dose and duration, a way to identify suitable recipients, and a means of detecting excessive or harmful effects. Important unresolved boundaries include preservation of nutritional adequacy, psychological well-being and appropriate responses to reduced energy availability. Durability would be valuable only if the resulting state remained safe and physiologically useful.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a relevant treatment-withdrawal result to Louis J. Aronne and colleagues’ SURMOUNT-4 randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA on 11 December 2023. It reports that, following initial tirzepatide treatment, mean weight change from week 36 to week 88 was −5.5% with continued tirzepatide and +14.0% after switching to placebo. These figures describe change over that interval; the +14.0% figure should not be interpreted as the percentage of previously lost weight regained or as change from the original pretreatment baseline.

Those trial details remain attributed to the supplied research rather than independently verified findings in this record. The validated review reports that the retained PubMed artifact contained only a cookie-access message, without the article title, authors, abstract or Results text. Consequently, that artifact could not confirm the intended article’s identity, numerical outcomes or study scope. The source index’s saved and verified flags do not resolve this content-access limitation. The limitation is a reason for qualification, not evidence that the reported trial result is false.

If confirmed as reported, the withdrawal result illustrates a limitation of that tirzepatide treatment strategy: continued treatment maintained and augmented weight loss on average, whereas withdrawal was followed by substantial regain. It would not establish that a durable regulatory reset is biologically impossible, nor would successful maintenance during ongoing treatment demonstrate such a reset.

The supplied materials contain no verified demonstration of the full proposed capability and no current field survey establishing its status in November 2026. The empty freshness record is separate from the access problem affecting the dated trial citation. Neither limitation supports a conclusion that the innovation has been achieved or that it cannot be achieved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized studies should show clinically meaningful improvements in prespecified metabolic and weight-related outcomes that persist for years after a time-limited endocrine intervention ends. A protocol could, for example, specify three to five years of follow-up after withdrawal, but that interval would be a proposed study-design choice, not an established standard. Studies should document treatment cessation, subsequent treatment use, retention and the distribution of outcomes rather than relying only on an average benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Clinically meaningful metabolic and weight-related benefits persist years after withdrawal

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal requirement: studies should provide evidence that the persistence reflects an altered regulatory response. Suitable comparisons and mechanistic measurements would need to distinguish that explanation from continuing drug effects, ongoing intensive support, persistent behavioral changes or anatomical effects. Behavioral contributions need not invalidate a useful therapy, but their presence would affect how confidently its benefits could be described as an endocrine reset.
completion_criteria.label: Evidence distinguishes altered regulatory responses from alternative causes of persistence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and adaptation requirement: evaluation should address nutritional adequacy, psychological well-being, compensatory hunger and relevant energy-regulation responses. Carefully bounded tests of ordinary changes in energy availability should examine whether the healthier state remains adaptable. The protocol should define adverse outcomes, rescue treatment and retreatment criteria before follow-up begins.
completion_criteria.label: Healthier regulation safely adapts to changes in energy availability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirement: independent studies should reproduce benefits across diverse, clearly characterized groups and report where effects are weak, absent or harmful. Practical assessment should include delivery burden, monitoring and the consequences of retreatment. Finite studies could establish demonstrated breadth within the populations and conditions tested; they could not prove literal universality or lifelong persistence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce benefits across diverse groups and report limits

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison based on the supplied roster: END-04, “A predictive theory of interacting endocrine control systems,” is closely related because a predictive account of hormonal interactions could help identify targets and interpret a lasting regulatory change. END-03, “An inexpensive continuous monitor for multiple human hormones,” could provide measurements useful for that work. A theory or monitor would be an enabling capability; neither would itself demonstrate durable resetting of energy balance.

Conceptual comparison based on the supplied roster: END-06, “Programmable tissue-selective control of hormone action,” overlaps with the challenge of producing targeted effects while limiting unwanted effects elsewhere. Tissue-selective control could potentially contribute to an intervention, but programmability and selectivity do not by themselves establish persistence after treatment ends.

Conceptual comparison based on the supplied roster: END-02, “A general platform for replacing failed endocrine glands with feedback-responsive tissue,” shares the ambition of restoring useful physiological feedback. END-01, “Immune-protected, renewable human islets that restore autonomous glucose regulation,” END-07, “Regenerate a person’s own functional pancreatic beta cells,” and END-08, “Restore ovarian endocrine function without previously banked tissue,” focus on restoring particular endocrine tissues or functions. END-05 instead concerns durable alteration of energy-balance regulation; tissue replacement or regeneration is not specified as its mechanism.

Conceptual comparison based on the supplied roster: END-09, “Glucose-responsive insulin that substantially automates insulin dosing,” concerns a treatment that adjusts insulin action to glucose conditions. It overlaps with the goal of adaptive regulation but does not imply that benefit persists after treatment withdrawal. END-10, “Induce durable antigen-specific tolerance in autoimmune endocrine disease,” shares the ambition of durable biological change, while targeting immune recognition rather than the mechanisms governing energy balance. These remain distinct innovations with different causal and safety demonstrations.

change_log.reason: It must not be confused with the fraction of prior weight loss regained or change from pretreatment baseline.

unresolved_issues: The retained PubMed artifact does not verify the intended trial’s identity, results or scope; the reported bibliographic and numerical details require accessible scientific text.
No supplied scientific source independently supports the broader regulatory framework, individual variation or the status of a universal resettable set point.
The freshness record is empty, so the supplied material cannot establish the field’s status in November 2026.
No specific endocrine target, intervention or causal mechanism for durable resetting is established by the supplied evidence.
The optimal follow-up duration, clinically meaningful outcome thresholds and measurements distinguishing regulatory change from other persistent effects remain to be specified.
The populations likely to benefit, long-term safety, retreatment needs and downstream disease outcomes remain unknown.

brief.title: Lasting, healthy weight control after treatment ends
possible: People with obesity could finish a short course of hormone treatment and keep lasting improvements in weight and health. Their bodies would maintain those benefits while allowing tolerable hunger, adequate nutrition and healthy responses when less food is available.
why: For people managing obesity and related health problems, this could reduce the need for continuing medication. Treatment could establish healthier control of appetite and energy use that sustains itself after medication ends.

sources.showed: Adults who stopped tirzepatide regained substantial weight, while those who continued treatment maintained and increased their weight loss.
sources.quote: In participants with obesity/overweight, withdrawing tirzepatide led to substantial regain of lost weight, whereas continued treatment maintained and augmented initial weight reduction.
sources.cited_for: The trial shows the difficulty of maintaining weight loss after this treatment stops.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate lasting changes in weight regulation after treatment or rule out achieving them with another approach.

sources.showed: In a small trial of people with HIV and excess abdominal fat, stopping semaglutide partly reversed improvements in weight, body fat and blood sugar control. Some weight benefit remained.
sources.quote: Discontinuation of semaglutide in PWH with lipohypertrophy resulted in partial loss of improvements in weight, adiposity, and metabolic parameters.
sources.cited_for: Benefits can partly persist after withdrawal even while weight and blood sugar control worsen.
sources.not_established: The trial does not establish benefits lasting years, safe adaptation to food shortages or effects across broader populations.

sources.showed: In a small trial of adults with obesity, semaglutide reduced hunger, food intake and weight during treatment compared with a dummy treatment.
sources.quote: Semaglutide reduced hunger and prospective food consumption, and increased fullness and satiety when compared with placebo
sources.cited_for: The trial shows that medication can change appetite and eating during treatment.
sources.not_established: It does not show that appetite changes persist after treatment or remain safe when food availability changes.

shown: Trials led by Louis J. Aronne and Ruth O. Adekunle show that stopping weight-loss medication can bring weight regain and loss of health benefits. Adekunle’s small trial found some weight benefit remained. Neither demonstrated a lasting, safe change in how the body regulates weight.
missing: A hormone treatment has yet to demonstrate meaningful weight and health benefits lasting years after it ends.
Studies must distinguish lasting changes in regulation from lingering drug effects, continued support or lasting changes in behaviour or anatomy.
The resulting state must preserve nutrition, psychological well-being and appropriate responses when less food is available.
Independent studies must establish who benefits, who is harmed and how much monitoring or repeat treatment is needed.

milestones.label: Weight and health benefits persist years after treatment
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials would have to show meaningful weight and health improvements lasting years after treatment ends. This would establish that benefits outlast medication.

milestones.label: Lasting benefits reflect changed regulation
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to distinguish altered appetite or energy-use responses from lingering drug effects, support, behaviour or anatomy. This would establish what sustains the benefit.

milestones.label: Healthier regulation stays safe as food availability changes
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to show adequate nutrition, psychological well-being, tolerable hunger and appropriate responses to changes in food availability. This would establish that lasting control remains adaptable.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce benefits and define their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce benefits across diverse groups and report harms, delivery burden and repeat-treatment needs. This would establish where the treatment works in practice.

uncertain: Which hormone targets could produce lasting changes, and would different people need different approaches?
How long should benefits persist, and which measurements would establish a meaningful change in regulation?
Long-term safety, repeat-treatment needs and effects on later disease complications remain unknown.

page.title: Drug-free remission of obesity after endocrine treatment
page.definition: A finite course of hormone-based treatment produces remission of clinical obesity—resolution of obesity-related organ dysfunction—after treatment ends, with a lasting change in appetite and energy-expenditure regulation. Nutrition, psychological health and responses to changes in food availability remain preserved.

goal.need: SURMOUNT-4, published on 11 December 2023, randomized 670 adults without diabetes after 36 weeks of tirzepatide and a mean weight loss of 20.9%. Subsequent withdrawal produced weight regain over 52 weeks, whereas continued treatment produced further loss. Maintaining benefit after treatment ends is a separate clinical objective.

figures.caption: SURMOUNT-4: mean weight change from week 36 to week 88
figures.note: Changes are relative to weight at randomization, not pretreatment weight or the amount previously lost. Both groups received lifestyle counseling.

statements.quote: Therapeutic strategies that target these mechanisms have the potential to reset the defended level of body weight at a lower, more normal value.
statements.context: The mechanisms discussed biologically defend elevated body fat; the statement supplies no withdrawal criterion.

statements.body: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases workshop
statements.quote: therapeutic strategies to alter the weight set point may be an important goal
statements.context: The workshop report describes discussion of changing the body weight defended by physiological responses.

statements.quote: In obesity, the goal is improving health in part through achieving a level and distribution of fat that optimizes body functions.

completion.title: A finite endocrine treatment induces drug-free remission by changing energy-balance regulation.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed controlled human study shows remission of clinical obesity for at least 6 months after a finite endocrine course, without continuing obesity medication and after pharmacological activity has ended. Mechanistic testing attributes maintenance to altered appetite and energy-expenditure regulation, distinguishes behavioral support and anatomical effects, and demonstrates retained responses to changes in energy availability. Nutrition, hunger and psychological outcomes meet prespecified clinical endpoints.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; the six-month clinical component comes from the Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission, but the combined mechanistic test is not an external standard.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA obesity-drug guidance, Endocrine Society statements, NIDDK workshop reports and published withdrawal trials found no completion criterion for a drug-free regulatory reset. This fallback uses the Commission's six-month remission definition and requires evidence of changed regulation with preserved adaptation. No external multiyear duration or numerical thresholds for adaptive responses or hunger were found.

milestones.title: A hormone treatment reduces laboratory meal intake versus placebo at 20 weeks.
milestones.criterion: In adults with obesity, energy intake at a freely eaten laboratory lunch after 20 weeks is lower than with placebo, using the protocol's two-sided 5% significance level. A phase 1 trial published on 2 December 2020 met this secondary endpoint: 72 adults (36 per arm) received semaglutide escalated to 2.4 mg weekly or placebo, yielding 1736 versus 2676 kJ (difference −940 kJ; P<0.0001). This establishes an on-treatment effect.
milestones.set_by: Novo Nordisk, NCT03842202; published semaglutide protocol endpoint and statistical test, rather than a general remission criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Energy intake during the ad libitum lunch was compared between semaglutide and placebo at week 20 as a secondary endpoint.

milestones.title: A hormone treatment exceeds control weight reduction by ≥5 percentage points after one maintenance-dose year.
milestones.criterion: After 1 year at the maintenance dosage, mean percentage weight reduction exceeds control by at least 5 percentage points, with a statistically significant difference. FDA's benchmark is draft, nonbinding guidance. STEP 1, published on 10 February 2021, randomized 1961 adults without diabetes. Its regimen included 16 escalation weeks and 52 maintenance weeks. Weight change was −14.9% with semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly versus −2.4% with placebo (estimated difference −12.4 percentage points; 95% CI −13.4 to −11.5; P<0.001). Both groups received lifestyle intervention.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, January 2025 draft guidance, section III.B.3.c; an on-treatment efficacy benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: the difference in mean percentage weight reduction between the investigational drug and control-treated groups is at least 5% and the difference is statistically significant.

milestones.title: A treatment recipient retains ≥80% of initial weight loss at 52 weeks after hormone withdrawal.
milestones.criterion: Retain at least 80% of weight lost during initial treatment at the assessment 52 weeks after withdrawal. SURMOUNT-4 used this individual responder threshold at week 88 after randomization at week 36: reported treatment-regimen estimates were 16.6% for switching to placebo versus 89.5% for continuing tirzepatide. This is a responder definition, not a population success threshold or evidence of altered regulation.
milestones.set_by: Eli Lilly and SURMOUNT-4 investigators, NCT04660643 key secondary endpoint; published for tirzepatide recipients in both randomized arms.
milestones.threshold_quote: maintaining at least 80% of the body weight loss during the 36-week open-label period

milestones.title: Obesity-related organ dysfunction resolves for ≥6 months without ongoing pharmacologic treatment.
milestones.criterion: Clinical manifestations of obesity-related organ dysfunction resolve for at least 6 months without requiring ongoing pharmacologic treatment. This endpoint does not establish changed regulation. A study published on 5 October 2026 randomized 108 adults with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy; 80 (39 semaglutide, 41 placebo) completed follow-up 24 weeks after withdrawal. Glycemic improvements were not sustained; one participant restarted semaglutide. The study did not assess the Commission's remission endpoint.
milestones.set_by: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission on clinical obesity, Table 1, consensus statement 8; a committee definition, not a validated regulatory-reset assay.
milestones.threshold_quote: sustained resolution (at least 6 months) of clinical manifestations of organ dysfunction without requiring ongoing pharmacologic treatment

not_found: No reset-specific preclinical advancement threshold was found.
ClinicalTrials.gov records rendered no endpoint text; trial endpoints were accessible in the published papers.
The PMC meal-study page and NEJM STEP 1 page were inaccessible; alternative full texts were accessible through the publisher and an institutional repository.
